# Engineers are shipping faster, so we made our CI self-driving to keep up


- [Raúl Negrón-Otero](https://posthog.com/community/profiles/43265)


Oct 28, 2026


- [AI](https://posthog.com/blog/ai)


,
- [Engineering](https://posthog.com/blog/engineering)


,
- [Developer experience](https://posthog.com/blog/developer-experience)


#### Contents


-
-
-
-
-


PostHog ships code at a rapid pace, and that pace has only accelerated in recent months due to LLM adoption. We went from merging 1,354 PRs in October 2025 to more than 6,500 PRs in October 2026 so far (an increase of more than 380%).


It's the job of the[Developer Experience team](https://posthog.com/teams/developer-experience)


to ensure engineers at PostHog are shipping as fast as possible while we work to balance code quality and CI stability. In fact, we have a goal of making[10,000 pull requests a month](https://posthog.com/blog/10k-prs-a-month)


easy. That said, it's difficult to keep up with CI maintenance just by observing and reacting manually.


So we took inspiration from how things are being shipped elsewhere at PostHog. This October, 11% of merged PRs were[self-driving](https://posthog.com/docs/self-driving)


, meaning PostHog opened them on its own after a[scout](https://posthog.com/docs/self-driving/scouts)


(a scheduled agent that explores your product data) found something worth acting on.


We saw this and decided to fight fire with fire. The same self-driving agents that are increasing our PR volume can help us keep up with CI maintenance. Here's how we set it all up:


##


Step 1: Get CI/CD data out of GitHub


We're proud to be open source and use[GitHub to host our monorepo](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog)


. This means most of our CI-related data lives on GitHub and is queryable from there. But querying this data frequently means we hit rate limits and, in any case, it would be really wasteful to constantly ask GitHub for mostly unchanging data (think last week's merged PRs and completed workflow runs). Above all, PostHog is a data company! So we decided to get CI/CD data into our own product and see what features and ideas we could unlock from there.


To accomplish this, we rely on our[GitHub warehouse source](https://posthog.com/docs/cdp/sources/github)


, which continuously syncs repository data. Specifically, we were interested in pull requests, workflow runs, and workflow jobs data.


##


Step 2: Add a queryable layer on the data (that agents can reach for)


We originally considered existing services to analyze CI data and help the DevEx team better understand developer behavior and pain points, but we found that most of these services were built around measuring engineering team productivity. That's not really what we were interested in.


Instead, we built our own internal product called Engineering Analytics. Its[core vision](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/blob/master/products/engineering_analytics/README.md#the-one-sentence-version)


is:


> It's product analytics, but the "users" are pull requests and the "events" are what happens to them on the way to production.


In building this, we benefited from the many data analysis, logic, and display primitives that other PostHog products had already built. We leaned on their best practices and just added CI/CD data and our own product needs.


Under the hood, Engineering Analytics is basically a curated view into the surfaces the DevEx team cares about: our CI system, the merge queue, and tests.


Besides being a useful place for engineers to quickly get a general sense for CI health, we included MCP support from the start so our agents could query for specific data when investigating CI troubles or looking for optimization opportunities. This way, agents don't need to rely on the GitHub API, and we can better control the data and agentic flows here. It also lets us build and use specific[skills](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/tree/master/products/engineering_analytics/skills)


like[investigating-ci-failures](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/tree/master/products/engineering_analytics/skills/investigating-ci-failures)


that help agents find the commit that broke a particular CI job, and then check whether a later commit fixed it.


##


Step 3: Make it self-driving


Engineering Analytics plugs into PostHog's[self-driving](https://posthog.com/docs/self-driving)


capabilities and generates its own["signals"](https://posthog.com/docs/self-driving/signals)


(findings along with their evidence), which agents then investigate autonomously and potentially attempt to remediate by opening pull requests.


These signals are generated from three deterministic detectors that run over the ingested GitHub data (each one is a pre-baked query):


-


**Flaky check** : a job that fails and then passes on a rerun of the same commit.


-


**Broken default branch** : a workflow that keeps failing on our main branch.


-


**Duration regression** : a workflow that got slower than it was in a previous window.


These detectors led to real fixes, like:


1. [Fixing a failing CI job](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/pull/95630)


: a WebKit Storybook shard was failing on every push to our default branch.
2. [Deflaking a Rust test job](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/pull/75826)


: the job flaked twice in one week (two tests were racing over shared tracing state).
3. [Speeding up a check on every pull request](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/pull/95082)


: a workflow job installed the whole workspace before a dry run that didn't really need any dependencies. After the fix, the whole job takes 33 seconds (down from 51 seconds).


Thanks to Engineering Analytics combined with self-driving, we've shipped more than a dozen related improvements since.


##


What we learned from building all this out


Finding the right signal-to-noise ratio requires some experimentation and a bit of prompt massaging. For us, having deterministic detectors has helped keep the signal-powered agents grounded in data we know we care about and expect to be continuously triaged.


Besides the utility of the MCP-first approach, Engineering Analytics's UI has gained traction inside the DevEx team, primarily as a "one-stop shop" where we can get a useful, at-a-glance look across our ownership surfaces. Because of this, we are working on optimizing product performance by moving from ad-hoc queries into pre-computed tables and otherwise optimizing our queries whenever possible. As an added bonus from both UI and MCP sharing the query layer, optimizations here also benefit the performance of agents reaching for these tools.


Finally, once we had GitHub and related CI data ingested, the team came up with other ways to build useful features around the data. As an example, we recently shipped a["CI Explorer" feature](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/pull/111949)


that graphs out our CI workflows. It's a lot more intuitive (not to mention faster) than clicking around the static GitHub UI.


##


How you can set up a self-improving CI yourself


We're continuing to shape Engineering Analytics as an internal beta product, but you can build something similar today by combining warehouse sources with our MCP and scouts. To do this:


1.


**Get your CI data into the warehouse.** Link the[GitHub source](https://posthog.com/docs/cdp/sources/github)


and sync the pull request, workflow run, and workflow job[tables](https://posthog.com/docs/cdp/sources/github#supported-tables)


. Add[webhooks](https://posthog.com/docs/cdp/sources/github#webhooks)


to keep runs and jobs up to date in real time.


2.


**Let your agent query it.** Connect your agent(s) to the[PostHog MCP](https://posthog.com/docs/model-context-protocol#get-started-in-30-seconds)


and try asking it something specific, like which CI workflow got slower this week.


3.


**Make it self-driving.**[Set up self-driving](https://posthog.com/docs/self-driving/setup)


and[connect the GitHub app](https://posthog.com/docs/libraries/github)


so agents can open pull requests on your behalf. Then, try writing a[scout](https://posthog.com/docs/self-driving/scouts#built-in-and-custom-scouts)


that watches your newly synced tables. Consider something like our deterministic detectors as a starting point, but there are more[ideas for custom scouts](https://posthog.com/docs/self-driving/scout-examples#ideas-for-custom-scouts)


in the docs.


Your CI/CD platform is already collecting all this data. You might as well put it to work for you!


> PostHog is your product's context layer. With a full suite of developer tools –[AI observability](https://posthog.com/ai-observability) ,[product analytics](https://posthog.com/product-analytics) ,[session replay](https://posthog.com/session-replay) ,[feature flags](https://posthog.com/feature-flags) ,[experiments](https://posthog.com/experiments) ,[error tracking](https://posthog.com/error-tracking) ,[logs](https://posthog.com/logs) , and more – PostHog ingests and stores all the data agents need to diagnose problems, uncover opportunities, and ship fixes. A[data warehouse](https://posthog.com/context-warehouse) and[CDP](https://posthog.com/cdp) tie it all together, unifying that context into one source agents can read across. You can steer it all from[Slack](https://posthog.com/slack) ,[the web app](https://posthog.com/ai) , the desktop ([PostHog Desktop](https://posthog.com/desktop) ), or your own editor via[the MCP](https://posthog.com/mcp) .
